title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 864–865 (Night 201, continuing nights-200), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 201 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The prince and Marzawān ride out into the open country, travel from morning to evening, rest and feed their beasts, and keep going for three days. On the fourth day they come to a broad place with a thicket, and there Marzawān carries out his ruse: he slaughters a camel and a horse, cuts up the flesh and hacks the bones, tears Qamar al-Zamān's shirt and drawers and cloak, smears them with the horse's blood and throws the cloak down where the road forks. When the prince asks what it is for, Marzawān explains: when King Shahramān rides out after them and finds the bloody clothes, he will believe his son killed by highwaymen or wild beasts, give up hope and go home, and they will be free to do what they mean to. Qamar al-Zamān praises the stratagem. They travel on for days and nights, the prince weeping and lamenting whenever he is alone, until the land they seek draws near and he recites four lines reproaching a beloved who forsakes a faithful lover. Then Marzawān points out the islands of King al-Ghayūr coming into view, and Qamar al-Zamān, overjoyed, thanks him, kisses him between the eyes and embraces him. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْأُولَى بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ūlā baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and first night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the first after the two hundred”: al-ūlā, “the first”, feminine of awwal, agreeing with layla; baʿda, “after”, puts al-miʾatayni, the dual of miʾa, “a hundred”, in the genitive. Night 200 was “the one completing the two hundred”; from here the count runs on in this way. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَمَرْزَوَانَ سَارَا وَاسْتَقْبَلَا الْبَرَّ وَسَافَرَا مِنْ أَوَّلِ النَّهَارِ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni wa-Marzawāna sārā wa-istaqbalā al-barra wa-sāfarā min awwali al-nahāri ilā al-masāʾi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān and-Marzawān went-they-two and-faced-they-two the-open-land, and-travelled-they-two from (the) first (of) the-day to the-evening.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān and Marzawān went on and set their faces toward the open country, and travelled from the beginning of the day until evening.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the last words of the night before, wa-istaqbalā al-barra, “and they set out toward the open country”. Both names are accusative after anna, and the verbs that follow are dual, sārā, istaqbalā, sāfarā, “the two of them went, faced, travelled”. sāfara, Form III, “to travel”. min awwali al-nahāri ilā al-masāʾi, “from the first of the day to the evening”: min marks where the span starts, ilā where it ends.

sentences.t: وَنَزَلَا وَأَكَلَا وَشَرِبَا وَأَطْعَمَا دَوَابَّهُمَا وَاسْتَرَاحَا سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَكِبَا وَسَارَا وَمَازَالَا سَائِرِينَ إِلَى ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-nazalā wa-akalā wa-sharibā wa-aṭʿamā dawābbahumā wa-istarāḥā sāʿatan thumma rakibā wa-sārā wa-mā zālā sāʾirīna ilā thalāthati ayyāmin
sentences.l: And-they-two-halted, and-ate, and-drank, and-fed their-two beasts, and-rested an-hour; then they-two-rode and-went, and-not-ceased-they-two going, to three days.
sentences.i: They halted, ate and drank, fed their beasts and rested a while; then they mounted and rode on, and kept going for three days.
sentences.n: A run of dual verbs, the two companions acting together. nazala, “to dismount, halt”. aṭʿama, Form IV, “to feed”; dawābb, plural of dābba, “beast of burden, mount”. istarāḥa, Form X, “to rest”; sāʿatan, “an hour”, that is a short while, accusative of time. The print sets mā zālā, “they did not cease”, solid as مازالا; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. mā zāla, “not to cease”, with its predicate in the accusative, sāʾirīna, “going”, the active participle of sāra in the plural where the dual sāʾirayni would be strict: Middle Arabic often lets the plural stand for two. ilā thalāthati ayyāmin, “up to three days”, “for three days”. The print writes ثلٰثة with the dagger alif, the old spelling without a written alif; it is kept. The ئ of سائرين is printed.

sentences.t: وَفِي رَابِعِ يَوْمٍ بَانَ لَهُمَا مَكَانٌ مُتَّسِعٌ فِيهِ غَابٌ فَنَزَلَا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī rābiʿi yawmin bāna lahumā makānun muttasiʿun fīhi ghābun fa-nazalā fīhi
sentences.l: And-in (the) fourth (of a) day appeared to-them-two a-place wide, in-it a-thicket; so-they-two-halted in-it.
sentences.i: On the fourth day a broad open place came into view, with a thicket in it, and they halted there.
sentences.n: rābiʿi yawmin, “the fourth of a day”, that is “the fourth day”: the ordinal set before an indefinite noun in the genitive. bāna li-, “to appear to”: li- marks those who see it. muttasiʿ, active participle of ittasaʿa, Form VIII, “to be wide, roomy”. fīhi ghābun, “in it a thicket”, a clause with no verb describing makānun. ghāb, “thicket, wood”, a collective whose single is ghāba. The shadda of متّسع is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ مَرْزَوَانُ جَمَلًا وَفَرَسًا وَذَبَحَهُمَا وَقَطَّعَ لَحْمَهُمَا قِطَعًا وَنَجَرَ عَظْمَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha Marzawānu jamalan wa-farasan wa-dhabaḥahumā wa-qaṭṭaʿa laḥmahumā qiṭaʿan wa-najara ʿaẓmahumā
sentences.l: And-took Marzawān a-camel and-a-horse, and-slaughtered-them-two, and-cut-up their-two flesh (into) pieces, and-hewed their-two bone.
sentences.i: Then Marzawān took a camel and a horse and slaughtered them both; he cut their flesh into pieces and hacked their bones.
sentences.n: The print has عظهما, a misprint for عظمهما, corrected here. ʿaẓm, “bone”, singular for the whole framework of bones, as laḥm is “flesh”. qaṭṭaʿa, Form II, “to cut up, cut to pieces”; qiṭaʿan, plural of qiṭʿa, “pieces”, an accusative of the result. najara is properly “to hew, plane (wood)”, said of a carpenter; on bones it must mean “chopped, hacked”. It is an unusual word here, and a slip for some other verb cannot be ruled out, but the print is kept and read so. The -humā, “of the two of them”, refers to the camel and the horse.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ مِنْ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ قَمِيصَهُ وَلِبَاسَهُ وَقَطَّعَهُمَا قِطَعًا وَلَوَّثَهُمَا بِدَمِ الْفَرَسِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha min Qamari al-Zamāni qamīṣahu wa-libāsahu wa-qaṭṭaʿahumā qiṭaʿan wa-lawwathahumā bi-dami al-farasi
sentences.l: And-he-took from Qamar al-Zamān his-shirt and-his-drawers, and-cut-them-two (into) pieces, and-smeared-them-two with-(the)-blood (of) the-horse.
sentences.i: He took Qamar al-Zamān’s shirt and drawers from him, cut them to pieces, and smeared them with the horse’s blood.
sentences.n: akhadha min, “to take from”: min marks the one it is taken from. libās, “clothing” in the old language, is in the Nights usually the drawers, the loose trousers worn under the robe, and that is the sense beside qamīṣ, “shirt”. lawwatha bi-, Form II, “to soil, smear with”: bi- marks what it is smeared with. The shadda of لوّثهما is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ جُبَّةَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَمَزَّقَهَا وَلَوَّثَهَا بِالدَّمِ وَرَمَاهَا فِي مَفْرِقِ الطَّرِيقِ ثُمَّ أَكَلَا وَشَرِبَا وَرَكِبَا وَسَافَرَا
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha jubbata Qamari al-Zamāni wa-mazzaqahā wa-lawwathahā bi-al-dami wa-ramāhā fī mafriqi al-ṭarīqi thumma akalā wa-sharibā wa-rakibā wa-sāfarā
sentences.l: And-he-took (the) cloak (of) Qamar al-Zamān and-tore-it and-smeared-it with-the-blood and-threw-it in (the) parting (of) the-road; then they-two-ate and-drank and-rode and-travelled.
sentences.i: He took Qamar al-Zamān’s cloak, tore it, smeared it with the blood, and threw it down where the road forks; then they ate and drank, mounted and journeyed on.
sentences.n: jubba, a long outer robe open at the front. mazzaqa, Form II, “to tear to shreds”. lawwatha bi- again, bi- for what it is smeared with. ramā, “to throw”, with the suffix -hā for the cloak. mafriq al-ṭarīq, “the parting of the road”, the fork where a road divides; mafraq is also said. Then the verbs turn dual again for the two travellers. The shaddas of جبّة, مزّقها and لوّثها are printed.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَمَّا فَعَلَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ مَا هٰذَا يَا أَخِي الَّذِي فَعَلْتَهُ وَمَا ذَا يُفِيدُ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾalahu Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿammā faʿalahu fa-qāla lahu mā hādhā yā akhī alladhī faʿaltahu wa-mā dhā yufīdu dhālika
sentences.l: So-asked-him Qamar al-Zamān about-what he-did-it, and-he-said to-him: What (is) this, O my-brother, which you-did-it, and-what (is) that (which) avails that?
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān asked him about what he had done, saying, “What is this you have done, brother? And what good will it do?”
sentences.n: saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿammā is ʿan + mā, “about what”. The -hu of faʿalahu and of faʿaltahu points back to mā and alladhī, “what” and “which”: Arabic repeats the object as a pronoun in such clauses. The print sets mā dhā, “what”, as two words, ما ذا, where the usual spelling is ماذا; it is kept, and read mā dhā. afāda, Form IV, “to be of use, avail”; yufīdu dhālika, “does that avail”. The hamza of فسأله is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ وَالِدَكَ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ إِذَا غِبْنَا عَنْهُ لَيْلَةً بَعْدَ اللَّيْلَةِ الَّتِي أَخَذْنَا بِهَا مِنْهُ الْإِذْنَ وَلَمْ نَحْضُرْ لَهُ فِيهَا يَرْكَبُ وَيُسَافِرُ فِي أَثَرِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu iʿlam anna wālidaka al-malika Shahramāna idhā ghibnā ʿanhu laylatan baʿda al-laylati allatī akhadhnā bihā minhu al-idhna wa-lam naḥḍur lahu fīhā yarkabu wa-yusāfiru fī atharinā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Know that your-father the-king Shahramān, when we-are-absent from-him a-night after the-night which we-took in-it from-him the-leave, and-not we-present to-him in-it, rides and-travels in our-track.
sentences.i: Marzawān answered, “Know that if we stay away from your father King Shahramān one night beyond the night for which we took leave of him, and do not come back to him in it, he will ride out and come after us on our trail.
sentences.n: Marzawān is the one who answers. anna wālidaka … yarkabu, “that your father … rides”: the subject stands first and the conditional idhā ghibnā … wa-lam naḥḍur, “if we are absent … and do not appear”, is set inside before its verb comes. After idhā the plain imperfect yarkabu, “he rides”, gives the result; a plain imperfect needs no fa- here, even in Classical. ghāba ʿan, “to be away from”: ʿan marks the one left. akhadhnā bihā minhu al-idhna, “we took in it from him the leave”: bi- here marks the time, “for which, on which”, a looser use than Classical; min marks the one who gives the leave. lam naḥḍur, jussive after lam. fī atharinā, “in our track”, on our trail. The shadda of انّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا وَصَلَ إِلَى هٰذَا الدَّمِ الَّذِي فَعَلْتُهُ وَرَأَى قَمِيصَكَ وَلِبَاسَكَ مُقَطَّعًا وَعَلَيْهِ الدَّمُ فَيَظُنُّ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُ جَرَى لَكَ أَمْرٌ مِنْ قُطَّاعِ الطَّرِيقِ أَوْ وُحُوشِ الْبَرِّ فَيَنْقَطِعُ رَجَاؤُهُ مِنْكَ وَيَرْجِعُ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ وَنَبْلُغُ بِهٰذِهِ الْحِيلَةِ مَانُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā waṣala ilā hādhā al-dami alladhī faʿaltuhu wa-raʾā qamīṣaka wa-libāsaka muqaṭṭaʿan wa-ʿalayhi al-damu fa-yaẓunnu fī nafsihi annahu jarā laka amrun min quṭṭāʿi al-ṭarīqi aw wuḥūshi al-barri fa-yanqaṭiʿu rajāʾuhu minka wa-yarjiʿu ilā al-madīnati wa-nablughu bi-hādhihi al-ḥīlati mā nurīdu
sentences.l: So-when he-arrives at this the-blood which I-made-it, and-sees your-shirt and-your-drawers cut-to-pieces and-on-it the-blood, then-he-thinks in himself that-it happened to-you a-matter from (the) cutters (of) the-road or (the) wild-beasts (of) the-open-land; so-is-cut-off his-hope of-you, and-he-returns to the-city, and-we-reach by-this the-stratagem what we-want.
sentences.i: When he comes upon this blood I have laid out, and sees your shirt and drawers cut to pieces with the blood on them, he will think to himself that something has befallen you at the hands of highwaymen or the wild beasts of the open country; then he will give up hope of you and go back to the city, and by this stratagem we shall reach what we want.”
sentences.n: idhā with perfects, waṣala, raʾā, looks to the future: “when he arrives … and sees”. muqaṭṭaʿan, “cut to pieces”, passive participle of qaṭṭaʿa, Form II, is singular though it describes two garments, and so is ʿalayhi, “on it”: the shirt and drawers are taken as one bundle. wa-ʿalayhi al-damu, “with the blood on it”, a clause of state. The answer begins with fa-, fa-yaẓunnu, “then he will think”; ẓanna fī nafsihi, “to think within himself”. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it befalls. quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq, “cutters of the road”, highwaymen. inqaṭaʿa, Form VII, “to be cut off”; rajāʾuhu minka, “his hope of you”. balagha bi-: bi- marks the means, “by this ruse”. The print sets mā nurīdu, “what we want”, solid as مانريد; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. The hamza of ورأى and of رجاؤه and the shaddas of مقطّعا and فيظنّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَاللّٰهِ إِنَّ هٰذِهِ حِيلَةٌ مَلِيحَةٌ نِعْمَ مَا فَعَلْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-Allāhi inna hādhihi ḥīlatun malīḥatun niʿma mā faʿalta
sentences.l: So-said Qamar al-Zamān: By-God, indeed this (is) a-stratagem fine; excellent (is) what you-did!
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said, “By God, this is a fine stratagem. Well done!”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, with the genitive. inna, “indeed”, follows the oath and strengthens the statement. malīḥ, “fine, pleasing”, a favourite word of the Nights for anything clever or comely. niʿma mā faʿalta, “excellent is what you did”: niʿma is the verb of praise, and mā, “what”, is the thing praised; the two are often written together as نعمّا, but the print sets them apart, and it is kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا سَارَا أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ كُلُّ ذٰلِكَ وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَشْتَكِي إِذَا انْفَرَدَ بِنَفْسِهِ وَيَبْكِي إِلَى أَنِ اسْتَبْشَرَ بِقُرْبِ الدِّيَارِ فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā sārā ayyāman wa-layāliya kullu dhālika wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni yashtakī idhā infarada bi-nafsihi wa-yabkī ilā an istabshara bi-qurbi al-diyāri fa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: Then indeed-they-two went days and-nights, all that, and-Qamar al-Zamān complains when he-was-alone by-himself, and-weeps, until that he-rejoiced at-(the)-nearness (of) the-abodes; so-he-recited, saying, these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then the two journeyed on for days and nights, and all that while Qamar al-Zamān would lament and weep whenever he was alone, until he took heart at the nearness of the land he sought, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: thumma innahumā, “then (it was that) the two of them”: inna opens the next step of the story. ayyāman wa-layāliya, “days and nights”, accusatives of time; layālī, plural of layla, takes only a fatḥa in the accusative. kullu dhālika wa-, “all that while, and …”: the clause with wa- tells what was going on throughout. ishtakā, Form VIII, “to complain, lament”. infarada bi-nafsihi, Form VII, “to be alone with himself”: bi- marks the company, here only himself. ilā an, “until”. istabshara bi-, Form X, “to rejoice at good tidings”: bi- marks the cause of joy. al-diyār, plural of dār, “abodes, lands”: the country where Budūr is. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”: the imperfect describes how he recited.

sentences.t:
اَتَجْفُو مُحِبًّا مَاسَلَا عَنْكَ سَاعَةً * وَتَزْهَدُ فِيْهِ بَعْدَمَا كُنْتَ رَاغِبًا
حُرِمْتُ الرِّضَى اِنْ كُنْتُ خُنْتُكَ فِي الْهَوَى * وَعُوقِبْتُ بِالْهِجْرَانِ اِنْ كُنْتُ كَاذِبًا
وَمَا كَانَ لِي ذَنْبٌ فَاسْتَوْجِبُ الْجَفَا * وَاِنْ كَانَ لِي ذَنْبٌ فَقَدْ جِئْتُ تَائِبًا
وَمِنْ عَجَبِ الْاَيَّامِ اَنَّكَ هَاجِرِيْ * وَمَازَالَتِ الْاَيَّامُ تُبْدِى الْعَجَائِبَا
sentences.tr:
a-tajfū muḥibban mā salā ʿanka sāʿatan * wa-tazhadu fīhi baʿdamā kunta rāghibā
ḥurimtu al-riḍā in kuntu khuntuka fī al-hawā * wa-ʿūqibtu bi-al-hijrāni in kuntu kādhibā
wa-mā kāna lī dhanbun fa-astawjibu al-jafā * wa-in kāna lī dhanbun fa-qad jiʾtu tāʾibā
wa-min ʿajabi al-ayyāmi annaka hājirī * wa-mā zālati al-ayyāmu tubdī al-ʿajāʾibā
sentences.l:
Do-you-treat-harshly a-lover (who) not was-consoled from-you an-hour, * and-you-lose-desire in-him after-what you-were desiring?
May-I-be-denied the-favour if I-was I-betrayed-you in the-passion, * and-may-I-be-punished with-the-forsaking if I-was lying.
And-not was for-me a-sin, so-I-deserve the-harshness; * and-if was for-me a-sin, then-already I-have-come repenting.
And-of (the) wonder (of) the-days (is) that-you (are) my-forsaker; * and-not-ceased the-days showing the-wonders.
sentences.i:
Will you be harsh to a lover who has not for one hour been consoled for you, * and turn from him in disdain, you who once desired him?
May I be denied your favour if I have betrayed you in love, * and punished with parting if I lie.
I have committed no sin, that I should deserve this harshness; * and if I have sinned, I have come to you repenting.
Among the wonders of the days is that you forsake me; * but the days have never ceased to bring wonders to light.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on rāghibā / kādhibā / tāʾibā / al-ʿajāʾibā, each with the long -ā that rounds off a rhyme in verse. The print sets mā salā, “has not been consoled”, solid as مَاسَلَا, and baʿdamā, “after”, solid as بَعْدَمَا, as usual; both are kept. a- asks the question; jafā, “to treat harshly, shun”. salā ʿan, “to be consoled for, forget”: ʿan marks what is forgotten. zahida fī, “to lose desire for”: fī marks what one turns from. ḥurimtu and ʿūqibtu are passive perfects used as a curse on oneself: “may I be denied … may I be punished”. al-riḍā, “goodwill, favour”, is printed الرِّضَى with ى, where the usual spelling is الرضا. bi-al-hijrāni: bi- marks the punishment, hijrān, “being forsaken”. In the third line the print points فَاسْتَوْجِبُ with a ḍamma, fa-astawjibu, “so I deserve”, and with the alif bare; after a denial with fa- the grammar would want the subjunctive fa-astawjiba, “that I should deserve”, but the print’s vowel is kept. istawjaba, Form X, “to deserve, merit”. jiʾtu tāʾiban, “I have come repenting”, tāʾib being the active participle of tāba, “to repent”. hājirī, “my forsaker”, active participle of hajara with the suffix “me”; the print sets a sukūn on its yāʾ, as it does on فِيْهِ, a mark of the long vowel. tubdī, Form IV of badā, “to show, bring to light”, is printed تُبْدِى with ى, the edition’s habit for final yāʾ. mā zālat … tubdī, “have not ceased showing”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ لَهُ مَرْزَوَانُ انْظُرْ هٰذِهِ جَزَائِرُ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ قَدْ لَاحَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha Qamaru al-Zamāni min shiʿrihi qāla lahu Marzawānu unẓur hādhihi jazāʾiru al-maliki al-Ghayūri qad lāḥat
sentences.l: And-when finished Qamar al-Zamān from his-verse, said to-him Marzawān: Look, these (are the) islands (of) the-king al-Ghayūr; already they-have-come-into-view.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān had finished his verses, Marzawān said to him, “Look: these are the islands of King al-Ghayūr, coming into view.”
sentences.n: faragha min, “to finish”: min marks what is finished. unẓur, imperative of naẓara, “look!”. jazāʾir, plural of jazīra, “island”: the realm of King al-Ghayūr, father of the Lady Budūr, is the islands and the seas. al-Ghayūr, “the Jealous”, is the king’s name and takes the article. qad lāḥat, “they have appeared”: qad with the perfect marks a thing just come about; lāḥa, “to come into sight, gleam”. The plural of things takes a feminine singular verb. The ئ of جزائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَشَكَرَ مَرْزَوَانَ عَلَى فِعْلِهِ وَقَبَّلَهُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَضَمَّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa Qamaru al-Zamāni faraḥan shadīdan wa-shakara Marzawāna ʿalā fiʿlihi wa-qabbalahu bayna ʿaynayhi wa-ḍammahu
sentences.l: So-rejoiced Qamar al-Zamān (with) a-rejoicing intense, and-thanked Marzawān for his-deed, and-kissed-him between his-two-eyes, and-embraced-him.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān was overjoyed; he thanked Marzawān for what he had done, kissed him between the eyes, and held him close.
sentences.n: fariḥa … faraḥan shadīdan, “rejoiced with a great joy”: the verbal noun of the same root heightens the verb. shakara ʿalā, “to thank for”: ʿalā marks what one is thanked for. fiʿl, “deed, doing”. qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”; bayna ʿaynayhi, “between his eyes”, on the forehead, a kiss of gratitude and honour; ʿaynayhi is the dual of ʿayn, “eye”. ḍamma, “to press to oneself, embrace”. The shaddas of قبّله and ضمّه are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
